### The Museum of Lost Sounds

On the third Tuesday of every month, a small museum opened beneath the old railway station, where the air smelled of rust, rain, and oranges.

The museum displayed sounds that had disappeared from the world: the click of a dial on a rotary telephone, the scrape of a chair across a wooden classroom floor, the first uncertain hiss of a radio warming up at night, coins dropping into the brass slot of a ticket machine.

Admission was free. Visitors were asked to bring one memory they had never spoken aloud.

At the center of the exhibition hung a glass case containing a narrow silver bell.

“This is the last sound of the original station announcement,” said the curator, an elderly woman with ink-stained fingers. “When the trains stopped running, the bell made one final chime. No one recorded it. Yet somehow, the museum received it.”

The curator invited each visitor to ring the bell. Most declined. Some rang it boldly. A nervous boy tapped it with his sleeve. An old man held it to his ear before striking it once.

After each chime, the museum became briefly quiet—not silent, but attentive, as if the whole building were listening for what had been lost inside the sound.

On my visit, I placed my memory in the case: the voice of my grandmother reading recipes aloud, each word slightly blurred because she had lost her sight. I did not tell the curator what it was. I only listened.

When the bell rang, I heard her.

Not a recording. Not a memory either. Her voice moved through the room with the clumsy tenderness of someone navigating a familiar kitchen in darkness.

“Two cups of flour,” she said. “One cup of sugar. And if you can’t find the vanilla, a little almond extract will do.”

Several visitors looked toward me.

I stood beside the glass, listening.

The voice continued, giving instructions no one had asked for, describing measurements by touch, warning that the stove ticked before it caught. Then she laughed at herself and murmured, “There. I’ve forgotten whether this is for the wedding cake.”

The sound faded.

In the case, the little bell trembled without being touched.

The curator smiled as if she had expected exactly this.

“Memories are strange things,” she said. “We think they disappear because no one is there to hear them. But sometimes they only wait for a room quiet enough to return.”

Outside, rain had begun falling over the station. It struck the roof in thousands of soft, silver notes.

For once, the city sounded new.
